BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) data for 5, 6, and 11 day incubation periods show values less than 1 mg/l in most cases and under 1.5 mg/l in all cases. Nitrogen and phosphorus values were low, as were concentrations of heavy metals. The concentrations of heavy metals present do not indicate pollution and would pose no water quality problems (Dysart, et al., 1973).
Figure 2-4 shows values for selected water quality parameters in Howard Creek (line graphs) and tributaries to Howard Creek (bar graphs). The dissolved solids content of Howard Creek increases with movement downstream (specific conductance and alkalinity). The greatest increases are noted below Bad Creek and West Bad Creek, and below Corbin Creek. Although pH varies from station to station, the mean levels remain constant throughout Howard Creek.
Seasonal variations occur in a number of parameters, most notably temperature and dissolved oxygen. Turbidity also appears to vary seasonally since the highest levels occur during the highest flow periods which are somewhat seasonal.
Figure 2-5 shows the Applicant's data for Howard Creek and five other tributaries to Lake Jocassee that were sampled at the confluence with the lake. (See Figure 2-14 for station locations.) Comparison of the data shows the water quality is very similar in most respects, although turbidity and some nutrient forms do show variations at some stations. In all cases, the water is low in alkalinity, total hardness, and dissolved solids, with acidic pH.
Aquatic Biota
Bad Creek, West Bad Creek, and Upper Howard Creek represent headwater drainage systems with heavily vegetated stream banks composed of rhododendron (Rhododendron spp.), American holly (Ilex opaca), alder (Alnus spp.), fetterbush (Lyonia spp.), and other forest understory species. Streams are heavily shaded in most sections. Aquatic habitats vary from waterfalls and cascades to riffles and pools. Intervening rock strata in the lower reaches of Howard Creek have caused the stream to form a series of stair-step pools and runs which terminate as the stream enters Lake Jocassee. Figures 2-6 through 2-10 depict stream conditions within the Howard Creek drainage during the winter of 1973.
